title: How Netflix Scaled Its Real-Time Service Map
gist: Netflix rebuilt the ingestion pipeline behind Service Topology — its real-time service dependency map — into three stages that separate intermediary resolution from enrichment and persistence, after hot instances hit up to 100x typical traffic. It propagates backpressure to Kafka instead of dropping records, swapped internal gRPC for server-sent events at high volume, and uses consistent hashing over a service-registry health list to rebalance without a separate rebalancing process.

insights.claim: Netflix's earlier Service Topology design concentrated work on popular destinations because intermediary resolution requires co-locating related flows, causing some instances to carry up to 100 times typical traffic while simultaneously doing I/O-heavy enrichment.
insights.speaker: Eran Stiller
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that graph-shaped workloads produce power-law hotspots that naive partitioning cannot absorb — a recurring failure mode to check in any dependency-graph or observability vendor's architecture.
insights.quote: some instances experienced up to 100 times the typical traffic while also performing I/O-heavy enrichment work
insights.locator: Netflix says its earlier design concentrated work

insights.claim: Separating intermediary resolution from enrichment and persistence into distinct pipeline stages is what allowed Netflix to redistribute hotspot work, making stage decomposition — not bigger instances — the fix for skewed graph processing.
insights.speaker: Eran Stiller
insights.so_what: A reusable design pattern: when one stage forces co-location and another is I/O-bound, splitting them decouples their scaling curves.
insights.locator: Separating resolution from enrichment and persistence

insights.claim: Netflix's network-flow pipeline runs three stages: consume multi-region Kafka streams and batch into five-minute windows, resolve intermediaries into direct application-to-application edges, then enrich nodes with health, ownership and metadata before persisting to a graph database.
insights.speaker: Eran Stiller
insights.so_what: Five-minute windowing is the real freshness floor for 'real-time' service maps at this scale — a useful benchmark when vendors claim sub-second dependency graphs.
insights.locator: Netflix therefore processes the data in three stages

insights.claim: Raw network flow records describe network hops rather than logical application dependencies because traffic traverses load balancers, NAT gateways, API gateways and proxies, so an intermediary-resolution step is mandatory to recover the true service graph.
insights.speaker: Eran Stiller
insights.so_what: Explains why eBPF-only observability products produce misleading topology maps without a resolution layer — a differentiator to probe in the observability vendor stack.
insights.quote: Raw flow records show network hops rather than the logical application dependency
insights.locator: The new post focuses on the network-flow ingestion path

insights.claim: Netflix uses Apache Pekko Streams so that when graph storage cannot keep up, backpressure travels upstream until the Kafka consumer pauses and records stay in Kafka until capacity returns, rather than being dropped.
insights.speaker: Eran Stiller
insights.so_what: Kafka is being used as the durable buffer of last resort, reinforcing its role as the non-negotiable substrate in high-scale streaming architectures.
insights.quote: pressure travels upstream through the processing stages until the Kafka consumer pauses, leaving records in Kafka until capacity returns
insights.locator: The pipeline uses Apache Pekko Streams to manage backpressure

insights.claim: Netflix explicitly trades freshness for completeness under load — accepting a delayed but complete dependency map over a fast but partial one — on the reasoning that an incomplete map during an incident is worse than a slightly stale one.
insights.speaker: Eran Stiller
insights.so_what: A correctness-over-latency stance that inverts the usual observability marketing pitch; useful lens for judging whether a tool is built for incidents or for dashboards.
insights.quote: The result is delayed freshness under load rather than dropped data or an incomplete map; Netflix considers that preferable to batch-generated maps that may already be stale during an incident.
insights.locator: The result is delayed freshness under load

themes.theme: gRPC dropped for internal high-volume transfer

insights.claim: Netflix replaced gRPC with server-sent events between internal pipeline stages after serialisation cost, connection-pool management and streaming-response memory pressure became expensive at its volume.
insights.speaker: Eran Stiller
insights.so_what: A notable counterexample to the default assumption that gRPC is the high-performance choice for internal RPC — the overhead profile flips at extreme streaming volumes.
insights.quote: serialisation, connection-pool management and streaming-response memory pressure became expensive at its volume
insights.locator: Netflix also replaced gRPC between pipeline stages

insights.claim: Netflix kept gRPC for the externally exposed Service Topology client API while swapping only the internal inter-stage transport to SSE, showing the transport decision is scoped per traffic profile rather than standardized org-wide.
insights.speaker: Eran Stiller
insights.so_what: Argues against monoculture transport mandates; the right protocol is a function of the specific hop's volume and streaming semantics.
insights.quote: This internal transport is separate from the gRPC API exposed to Service Topology clients.

insights.claim: Netflix's processing fleet scales elastically by having each instance read the same current list of healthy instances from the service registry and apply consistent hashing to determine aggregator ownership, so joins and departures move only affected aggregators with no separate rebalancing process.
insights.speaker: Eran Stiller
insights.so_what: A pattern for eliminating an entire class of coordination machinery — worth checking whether competing platforms still carry a stateful rebalancer as operational debt.
insights.quote: the updated list automatically moves only the affected aggregators to new owners, without a separate rebalancing process
insights.locator: Each instance reads the same current list

insights.claim: The IPC metrics pipeline needs no intermediary-resolution stage because its data already describes application-level calls and arrives partitioned by application, so it aggregates in a single stage — the data source's native shape determines pipeline complexity.
insights.speaker: Eran Stiller
insights.so_what: Instrumenting at the application layer removes downstream reconstruction cost — an argument for investing in first-party instrumentation over inferring topology from network telemetry.
insights.locator: The IPC pipeline does not need this extra redistribution step

insights.claim: Rather than retaining complete graph snapshots or replaying an event log, Netflix stores time-windowed aggregator snapshots plus property-level mutation history to reconstruct the service topology at any specified point in time.
insights.speaker: Eran Stiller
insights.so_what: A storage-cost-efficient middle path between snapshotting and full event sourcing; relevant to anyone pricing retention for historical observability data.
insights.locator: The post also describes historical reconstruction

insights.claim: Service Topology merges three independently stored views — eBPF network flows, inter-process communication metrics, and distributed traces — that can be queried separately or combined, and Netflix teams use it for incident investigation, blast-radius analysis, dependency understanding and production change management.
insights.speaker: Eran Stiller
insights.so_what: Multi-source graph fusion is the emerging requirement bar for service maps; single-signal observability products are structurally below it.
insights.locator: Service Topology combines separately stored views
